title: Translatio Homiliarum XXXIX Origenis In Evangelium Lucae
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp482.tmp482.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Quamobrem petatis, ul contemptis istiusmodi nugis, saltem b triginta et novem Adamantii nostri in Lucam homilias, sicut in Graeco habentur, inter- preter : molestam rem et tormento similem, alieno, ut ait Tullius, stomacho et non suo scribere : quam tamen idcirco nunc faciam, quia sublimiora non poscitis. Siquidem illud quod olim Romae sancta Blaesilla flagitaverat, ut c viginti quinque tomos il- lius in Matthaeum, et quinque alios in Lucam, et d triginta duos in Joannem, nostrae linguae traderem, nec virium mearum, nec otii, nec laboris est.
passages.english: For this reason you ask that, setting aside trifles of this sort, I should at least translate the thirty-nine homilies of our Adamantius on Luke, just as they are found in the Greek: a troublesome thing, and like torture, to write, as Tully says, with another's stomach and not one's own. Yet I will do it now for this reason, that you do not ask for loftier things. For what the holy Blaesilla once urgently asked of me at Rome, that I should render into our language his twenty-five volumes on Matthew, and five others on Luke, and thirty-two on John, is beyond my strength, my leisure, and my capacity for labour.
passages.notes: 'ul' read as 'ut'; stray letters b, c, d are footnote marks and are omitted. 'Adamantius' is Origen; 'Tully' is Cicero. The last clause is literally 'is neither of my strength, nor of my leisure, nor of my labour'.

passages.original: Si videris haereticos dogmatum suorum menda- cium pro pane comedere, scito lapidem eorum esse sermonem, quem monstrat diabolus. Neque vero existimes unum eum habere lapidem; habet plures lapides, de quibus a Matthaeo introducitur loquens : Dic ut lapides isti panes fiant. Dixit et Marcion, et lapis diaboli ei factus est panis. Dixit Talentinus, et alius lapis ei est versus in panem. Habuit et Basi- lides ejusmodi, et caeteri haeretici. Unde sollicite providendum, ne forte diaboli lapidem comedentes, putemus pane vesci Dei.
passages.english: If you see heretics eating the lie of their doctrines in place of bread, know that their teaching is the stone which the devil shows. And do not suppose that he has only one stone; he has many stones, about which Matthew introduces him speaking: "Tell these stones to become loaves." Marcion spoke, and the devil's stone became bread for him. Valentinus spoke, and another stone was turned into bread for him. Basilides too had [a stone] of this kind, and so did the other heretics. Hence we must take careful precautions, lest perhaps, while eating the devil's stone, we think we are feeding on the bread of God.
passages.notes: "Talentinus" is evidently a scanning error for "Valentinus" (the Gnostic teacher, named alongside Marcion and Basilides) and is translated as such.
